justification: The two designs are nearly identical short letters. In A1 the justified first line has noticeably wide word gaps. B1 sets the same text with tighter, more even spacing in a slightly sturdier serif. B1 also adds a thin rule at the top, which gives the page a more finished letterhead feel. The difference is small.

Both designs are nearly identical single-page invoices. A's navy title band gives the invoice number a stronger anchor and clearer hierarchy than B's plain serif heading. B's quieter serif look is elegant but flatter. A's header bar repeats the title redundantly, a minor flaw.

The two letters are nearly identical in layout. B's serif text has slightly stronger contrast and reads more like a formal letter. A's light grey sans is somewhat faint. A's heavy navy top band adds some brand presence, but it isn't needed. Both leave most of the page empty in the same way.

Both memos are near-identical one-page layouts with a dark header band and short body text. A's justified body opens large word gaps in the 'Parking permits…' line, leaving a visibly gappy, rivered line. B's ragged-right serif text sets evenly, giving smoother reading rhythm. Header bands are comparable.

Both are short letters with the same layout. A's justified first line produces visibly wide word gaps, while B's ragged-right sans text sets evenly. B also adds a subtle navy top band that gives the page some identity. Neither has a header block, so the hierarchy is equal.

In A the headings hang far left of the indented body text, and a rule sits above every section. This produces ragged left edges and an over-divided page. B uses one consistent left margin shared by headings, body and table. Its numbered headings and calmer navy band give a cleaner, more coherent column. A's lighter text is also harder to read.

A orphans the single 'Next Steps' section onto a nearly empty second page (A2), leaving a wasted page and a broken flow. B fits every section on one page (B1). Its bold sans headings stand out clearly, and the indented body text gives a steady rhythm. A's serif headings are elegant, but its body text is small and light.

A uses a solid title band whose edges match the table and body margins, so the page reads as one aligned column. A's top header repeats the invoice number in both corners, which is redundant. B's heading hangs left of the indented body and table. Its thin rule runs to a different width, which leaves the alignment ragged. B's serif text is pleasant, but its structure looks less resolved.

Both are short letters on a mostly empty page. A uses an even ragged-right sans with natural word spacing and a thin navy top band that gives a letterhead feel. B justifies a two-line paragraph, which opens visibly wide word gaps in the first line, and B has no framing element.

B separates sections with hairline rules and indents body text and the table under hanging headings, which gives a clearer, more structured cadence down the page and fills the sheet more evenly. A uses numbered headings that help navigation, but its flush-left stack feels plainer and leaves a heavier empty bottom. B's brighter blue header is slightly less refined than A's navy. Overall B reads as more organised.

Both letters sit at the top of a mostly empty page. A's ragged-right serif setting keeps word spacing even. B's justified paragraph shows visibly stretched word gaps in its first line. A's thin navy top rule adds a modest letterhead accent that B lacks.

The two letters are nearly identical. B sets the text ragged-right in a refined serif with even word spacing. A justifies the opening paragraph, which stretches the word gaps visibly. A's "Page 1 of 1" footer is also unnecessary. B's full-bleed rule is a little heavier but works as a clean letterhead accent.

In A the headings hang outdented to the left of the rules and body text, and the code blocks sit at yet another indent, which leaves the left edge ragged. A's bold headings are stronger, but B aligns its headings, body text and rules on one consistent left axis, giving a cleaner and more coherent column.

A fits the whole proposal on one page, and its bold sans headings stand out clearly. B pushes the short Next Steps section alone onto a second page, which is almost entirely empty (B2). That leaves an awkward gap at the bottom of B1 and weakens balance. B's light serif headings also give a weaker hierarchy than A's.

A fits all six sections on one balanced page. B spills only the final 'Next Steps' section onto a nearly empty second page, leaving a large void at the bottom of B1. Most of B2 is blank, which fragments the document's ending. The two designs' typography differs only in style (sans vs serif); both read cleanly.

The two designs share the same layout and navy header band. B sets the body in a serif with darker, more legible text and slightly larger leading. A's light grey sans body reads faintly. A's justified 'Parking permits' line also shows wider word gaps than B's.

A uses bold, numbered section headings that stand out clearly from the serif body text. B's light-weight headings are close in tone to its body text and lean on rules for separation, which makes the hierarchy weaker. In B the rules also sit oddly close to the code blocks. A has better spacing rhythm.

A keeps headings, rules and body on one consistent left edge with a cohesive serif pairing. In B the bold sans headings hang out to the left of the rules and text, and the code blocks overshoot the rules on the right, so the edges look misaligned. B's bolder headings are more prominent, but A's alignment and rhythm read cleaner.

The two designs are nearly identical in layout. A sets the body in a serif with more even spacing, apart from its last justified line. B's light sans body is justified across the full width, which opens wide gaps in both paragraphs, most visibly in the 'Parking permits' line. That makes B's text texture blotchier and slightly harder to read.

A has a stronger bold sans title. However, its title hangs left of the content column, and the bill-to line, table and totals are indented. That leaves a ragged left edge and a misaligned rule. B keeps the title, table and totals on one consistent left margin. Its top band and rule frame the page coherently, so its structure is tidier even though the title is lighter.

Both designs share the same structure. B justifies its text, which opens wide rivers in the second paragraph ("Parking permits for the new building…") because the long email address is pushed to the next line. A sets the text ragged-right in an even serif with consistent word spacing, so it reads cleanly. The header bands are comparable.

The layouts are nearly identical. A pairs a bold sans title with clean sans headings and body, which suits a CLI manual and matches the monospace code. B's light serif body is thin and small, and reads less crisply beside the code blocks. B's slightly looser line spacing is a minor plus, but A's text is clearer overall.

A's bold sans headings give stronger section hierarchy, but its headings hang left of the rules and body text while code blocks overshoot the right margin, creating ragged, misaligned edges. B keeps headings, body, rules and code blocks on a consistent left edge with a calmer serif rhythm; its light headings are weaker but still clear.

The two designs share the same content and layout. B's solid navy title band gives the invoice heading stronger emphasis and a clearer document identity. A's serif title is quieter and reads as more understated. B's header band repeats the invoice number on both sides, which is slightly redundant, but its overall hierarchy is clearer. A's serif styling is refined but weaker as an invoice heading.

Both pages carry the same short letter. A sets its body text fully justified, which opens visibly loose word gaps in the first line ("Thank you for your application for the Senior Analyst position"). B is ragged-right with even word spacing in a refined serif. B's thin navy top rule also frames the page and gives the letter a finished, letterhead feel.

Design A's justified text leaves huge word gaps in the 'Parking permits…' line, where the email address breaks onto the next line. Design B uses ragged-right serif text with even spacing and reads cleanly. The header bands and the overall layout are comparable.

B aligns the title band, bill-to line, table and totals on one consistent left edge, giving a tidier structure. In A the content is indented under a heading that sits further left, which reads as misaligned. B's header bar repeats the same invoice number on both sides, which is redundant, but its title band anchors the page well. A's serif type and plain title are elegant, but the inconsistent indents weaken its balance.

The two pages are nearly identical short letters. B's serif face suits a formal letter and reads slightly better than A's light grey sans. B's thin top rule is also more restrained than A's heavy top band. Both leave the lower page empty in the same way.

Design A pushes a single short 'Next Steps' section onto a second page that is otherwise empty, which leaves a lopsided, wasteful layout. Design B fits all six sections on one page. Its bold, numbered sans headings give clearer hierarchy than A's light, rule-separated headings, and the section spacing is even throughout.

A aligns the heading, bill-to line, table and totals on one consistent left edge. B outdents its heading past the body column, which gives a ragged, misaligned left edge, and its light condensed body face is slightly harder to read. A does carry a stray '1' section number in the title and a redundant running header, but its alignment is cleaner overall.

B's bold, numbered sans headings stand clearly apart from the serif body text. A's light serif headings are close in weight to the body, and its rules are repeated before every section, so the section breaks feel weaker. B's body text is also slightly larger and easier to read.

Both designs have the same content and table structure. B numbers the title "1 Invoice" and repeats the invoice number in a running header ("1 Invoice INV-2026-0142"), which is redundant and odd for a one-page invoice. A has a cleaner title with a refined serif, a simple top band, and a minimal footer. B's bold sans heading gives a stronger contrast, but the numbering makes it look like an auto-generated report.

B adds an artefactual "1" section number to the invoice title and a redundant running header, which clutter the hierarchy. A's title is clean, with a rule above it. A does indent the body and table oddly from the title, but its heading is more correct.

The two designs are nearly identical in structure. A's serif type gives the manual a more refined, bookish character. It also spaces its sections a little more generously, so the rhythm between rule, heading and code block is calmer. B's sans-serif is clean and readable but feels tighter, and its sections crowd together slightly.

Both designs lay out the same single-page invoice with near-identical tables. A has a stray "1" section number in both the title and the running header, and its header repeats the invoice number redundantly. B has a cleaner title, a refined serif, and a top band with rule that frames the page neatly. A's bold sans heading gives slightly stronger hierarchy, but its numbering artifacts detract from it.

Both layouts are nearly identical and share the same justified-text gaps in the parking line. A's muted navy band reads calmer and more businesslike than B's saturated royal blue. A's heading and serif body pair a bit more cohesively. B's letter-spaced body text is slightly lighter and looser, which weakens readability a little.

The two designs are nearly identical in layout. Each has a full-width colour band with the title, a three-line header block and two justified paragraphs. In B, the light sans body text set tight sits on a narrower measure. Its justified last paragraph line shows wider word gaps ("Parking permits for the…"). A's serif body text has a slightly warmer, more readable texture. Both share the large empty lower page.

B's bold heavy section headings stand out clearly against the indented serif body, giving a stronger hierarchy. A's light-weight headings are close in tone to its body text, so the sections read flatter. B's title, though, is indented differently from its outdented headings, and its code blocks overhang the rules. A is more aligned, but its structure is weaker overall.

The two letters are nearly identical. A is set ragged-right in a refined serif. B justifies the first paragraph, which opens visibly loose word gaps on such a short line. A also has a slightly stronger top rule. Both leave the page mostly empty below the signature.

A keeps a single clean left edge: the title, the rules, the headings, the body and the table all share one margin, so the page reads calmly. Its navy band and consistent sans type feel cohesive. B's headings are bolder and give stronger hierarchy. But B indents the body and table well past the headings, and the title sits at a different inset than the rules. This creates three competing alignment lines and leaves the page feeling left-heavy and fragmented. B's small serif body text is also lighter and harder to read.

Both are the same short letter crowded at the top of an otherwise empty page, with no letterhead, date, or spacing to set off the closing and signature. A sets its serif text justified, which opens visible gaps in the first line. B uses ragged-right sans text with even word spacing. B's solid navy top band gives the page a firmer identity than A's thin hairline rule.

The two designs are nearly identical: same structure, a full-width header band, a short memo body, and a large empty lower page in both. A uses a bright royal blue band with Montserrat-style headings. B uses a darker navy band with a slightly larger serif body. Both justified paragraphs leave the same wide gaps in the 'Parking permits' line. Neither is meaningfully better.

A's headings hang out to the left of the title and body indent, and the rules run past the text while the code blocks overshoot them, so the edges are ragged. B keeps one left edge from the title through the headings, body text and code blocks. Its numbered headings and calm navy band read more cohesively. A's rules do add some section separation.

B uses bold numbered sans headings that stand out clearly against a serif body, giving stronger hierarchy and easier scanning. A's light-weight headings with rule lines above each section feel thin and fragmented, and its light grey sans body text is weaker in contrast. The banner and code blocks are equivalent in both.

The two designs are nearly identical in layout. In B, the serif body text has slightly more comfortable leading and reads more easily than A's light sans body. Both share the same justified-line gap in the parking sentence. B's brighter blue band and geometric heading pair well with the serif body. A's navy band is more restrained but its thin body text is weaker.

A keeps a single consistent left margin for headings, body, and code blocks, and its numbered headings aid navigation. B pulls its headings out into the gutter while body text sits indented. Its code blocks start at yet another edge and overshoot the rule lines on the right, giving a ragged, misaligned column. B's saturated blue band is louder than A's restrained navy.

The two letters are nearly identical. A's serif face sets more evenly, with tighter, more even word spacing in the justified paragraph. A also has a thin rule at the top that gives the page a finished letterhead feel. B's justified first line shows visibly wide word gaps, and the page has no framing element. Both leave a lot of empty space below the short text.

A fits all six sections on one page with bold numbered headings, which gives a clear hierarchy and a compact rhythm. B gives every section a rule and extra spacing, so the short final 'Next Steps' section spills onto a nearly empty second page, an orphaned layout that wastes space. B's light serif headings are also weaker than A's bold sans headings.

Both memos share the same layout and header band. A justifies its second paragraph, which leaves large rivers of space in "Parking permits for the new building" because the long email address won't break. B sets the text ragged-right with even word spacing and a cohesive serif title, though its body type is slightly small and light.

Both are near-identical one-page memos with a header band. B justifies its last paragraph, so the line 'Parking permits for the new building will be issued on arrival. Contact' is stretched into wide rivers of space. A sets its text ragged-right, keeping word spacing even and the text easier to read. A's serif headline on a dark band also pairs cohesively with its body text.

Design A uses bold, numbered sans headings over serif body text, which gives clear contrast and an easy-to-scan hierarchy. Design B sets its headings in a light weight, with a rule above every section. The rules near the table stack up into doubled lines and add clutter, and the thin headings carry less weight. Layout and the header band are otherwise nearly identical.

A keeps a consistent left margin: the title, bill-to line and table all align. Its top band and rule frame the page cleanly. In B the bold sans title hangs outdented past the body column, and the rule extends beyond the table. This gives B a ragged left edge and mismatched type pairing. B's bolder title does give slightly stronger emphasis, but A's alignment reads as more polished.

Both designs are near-identical one-page memos with a dark header band. B's justified final paragraph opens wide rivers of space between words ('Parking permits for the new building will be issued on arrival.'), which hurts readability. A's ragged-right setting avoids this. A also has slightly more generous spacing between the header and the body.

The two designs are nearly identical in content and table layout. A's navy title band gives the invoice a clear, branded heading. B shows a stray section number, "1 Invoice", in both its title and its header, which looks like an artifact on an invoice. B's serif body text is pleasant, but the stray numbering tips the balance toward A.

A's bold sans numbered headings stand out clearly against the serif body and make the sections easy to scan. B's light serif headings sit under rule lines and carry less weight, which weakens the hierarchy. B's body text is also smaller and lighter, so it is harder to read. Otherwise the layouts are nearly identical.

Design B fits all sections on a single page. Design A pushes the one-line 'Next Steps' section onto a second page that is otherwise almost empty, which wastes space and breaks the flow. The two designs are otherwise very similar in styling. A's serif type is slightly smaller and lighter.

B aligns its headings, body text and table on one consistent left edge, giving a cleaner, more coherent column. A hangs its headings at the margin and indents body and table under them, which reads less tidy, and it pairs a serif body with a sans heading. A's bolder headings give slightly stronger hierarchy, but B's light headings are still clear.

The two designs share nearly the same content and table structure. Design A has a stray "1" section number in the title and in the running header, which is odd on an invoice. Design B drops that numbering and puts the title in a solid navy band, matched by a header band, so it reads as a more finished and branded invoice. A's serif text is slightly easier to read, but B's sans is clean. Both designs leave most of the page empty.

The two pages are nearly identical in structure. A's serif face suits a formal letter and reads with darker, firmer text. B's light sans is thin and grey, which slightly weakens contrast, and its heavier top band adds little. The difference is marginal.

B's bold numbered headings stand clearly apart from the serif body text, so the sections are easy to scan. A uses light-weight headings in the same sans as the body and adds a rule above every section. The result is weaker contrast, and the rules fragment the page. The tables and header bands are essentially the same in both.
